source.title: An alternative approach to train neural networks using monotone variational inequality
source.authors: Chen Xu; Xiu-Yuan Cheng; Yao Xie

record.tranche_reason: The study reports train and test performance under several architectures and widths, including results where the methods differ in generalization; it does not test memorization of random labels or the mapped interventions directly.
record.gate_note: Relevant rows report training-versus-test performance for the study's SVI and SGD methods, and width comparisons. These are not direct tests of random-label memorization, the optimizer comparisons in V4, fixed-epoch large-batch penalties, dropout, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. No random-label results are reported.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates its proposed SVI training method against SGD, but none of its results tests V1–V8. Width comparisons do not establish generalization beyond interpolation: training errors remain substantial, and networks are compared at fixed epochs rather than convergence. SVI is not an adaptive optimizer of the kind named in V4. The study does not rely on a listed finding as an experimental tool, so T4 also does not apply.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors establish prediction guarantees for last-layer training with frozen earlier layers under their assumptions, and report faster early convergence with competitive or better final performance than SGD in their experiments. Their multi-layer extension is heuristic and does not inherit the last-layer guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: SVI replaces the gradient update direction with a vector field constructed from a monotone variational inequality; the comparisons use matched data, architecture, loss, initialization, hyperparameters and training regime. This differs from the claim versions' interventions and measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the benefit varies by task and stage: SVI improves early convergence; MNIST uses a SVI-then-SGD hybrid because gradient-based methods may be preferable for optimal performance after the initial stages. Traffic GNN improvements are small for 64 and 128 hidden neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: SVI achieves lower prediction losses or errors than SGD on synthetic probit and GNN tasks and generally improves solar and traffic classification metrics; traffic gains are small at widths 64 and 128.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Replacing gradient updates with the proposed SVI updates can improve predictive performance under the paper's matched experimental settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Wider ogbn-arxiv GNNs achieve higher test accuracy at fixed training budgets, and SVI outperforms SGD at each tested width. Training accuracy remains far below perfect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing GNN width can improve predictive performance before interpolation at fixed epoch budgets.

fits_no_version.finding: SVI followed by SGD improves initial convergence and final MNIST metrics relative to SGD; SVI is described as competitive on CIFAR-10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SVI can provide an effective initial training phase or competitive alternative to SGD for the tested image classifiers.

record.problems: The study is not designed to test the listed claim versions. The image-classification numerical results are figure-only in the supplied text; experiments are averaged over three random trials, with uncertainty shown as standard errors or standard deviations. Some traffic GNN differences are small.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported result rows were omitted; figure-only numerical values are not recoverable from the text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting, natural-label generalization under the same recipe, and chance-level held-out performance with random labels.
Test-error behavior when widening beyond a demonstrated zero-training-error threshold under training to convergence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers, the contribution of local connectivity, and initialization or sparsity conditions.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning, decoupled weight decay, and switching from Adam to SGD.
Large versus small batches under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes that affect their generalization difference.
Dropout interventions, training-set-size dependence, excessive dropout, and removal of dropout and weight decay with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Identification and removal of memorized examples, retraining, and comparison with random-example removal.

record.verdict_notes: All row states are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because the rows measure different comparisons; this does not dispute the reported SVI advantages. These method-performance rows should not serve as evidence for the listed claims. No omitted result in the supplied text warrants a verdict on a listed version.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence are not tested.
No one-hidden-layer width sweep around the zero-training-error threshold is reported.
No convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison isolating local connectivity is reported.
The paper compares SVI with SGD, not adaptive optimizers such as Adam with SGD under the specified tuning conditions.
No large-batch versus small-batch generalization comparison under fixed epoch budgets is reported.
Dropout and weight-decay interventions are not tested.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or competing generalization measures are measured.
The study does not identify/remove memorized examples or compare against random-example removal.
